extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy of science, logic, and methodology
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and practical tests for judging theories of causation and causal explanation in natural philosophy; addresses when hypotheses are legitimate, what counts as a cause, and how to distinguish genuine causal relations from mere concomitance or subjective intuition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vera causa requirement for hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: A supposed cause invoked in explanation should be a vera causa (a genuine cause); hypotheses must posit a real causal agent rather than mere fanciful entities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poincaré notes that explanations may contain hypotheses but insists the supposed cause should be a vera causa (example: attributing intestinal motion of molecules as a vera causa). This is presented as a test of legitimacy for explanatory hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary ad hoc suppositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Theories should not rely on gratuitous auxiliary assumptions (e.g., postulating a subtle ether) unless warranted by independent evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text criticizes the introduction of an ether to transfer heat from the sun as an extra hypothesis needed to reduce conservation of force to conservation of motion; such suppositions may be legitimate as hypotheses but are suspect if added solely to force a particular reduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct conceptual definition of force (potentiality vs actual motion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions must capture the true nature of the concept: force is better defined as a potentiality of motion rather than necessarily as actual motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: since bodies may not be in actual molecular motion while still capable of producing motion when collocated appropriately (coal, lifted stone), force should be understood as potential motion; conceptual precision prevents category mistakes in causal analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causation as invariable, unconditional sequence of antecedents and consequents
rubrics_metrics.description: A cause is the set (or sets) of antecedent conditions which are invariable and unconditionally followed by the phenomenon (the consequent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poincaré frames causation formally: whether called transformation or generation of force, the phenomenon has antecedent sets that constitute its cause by virtue of their invariable sequence with the effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish presence of force and collocation of objects in causal conditions (Bain's two-element test)
rubrics_metrics.description: In analysing causes, separate the element that is a force (something changing) from the collocation/arrangement of objects required for the force to produce the particular effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: to produce a bonfire you need both combustible materials (collocation) and chemical action (force); to grind corn you need mill parts arranged properly (collocation) and moving water or wind (force). The collocation often implicitly includes objects possessing the force-giving property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of causation: change can only be produced by change (need for a changing antecedent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any causal account must include at least one antecedent that is itself changing (a force); mere stationary collocations without a changing antecedent cannot produce change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poincaré emphasizes that alongside stationary antecedents there must be a changing antecedent to produce phenomena — this frames causal adequacy tests for proposed causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expenditure or transfer of energy as a practical test distinguishing causation from concomitance
rubrics_metrics.description: When an effect consists in putting matter in motion, the true cause can be identified among antecedents by noting which antecedent has lost motion (i.e., expended or transferred energy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Following Bain (endorsed here), if an object present has lost motion corresponding to the motion manifested in the effect, that object has contributed causally — this supplies an empirical sign of causal contribution where motion/energy transfers are involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejecting volition-as-sole-cause absent external evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: One must not accept the doctrine that Mind/Will is the only efficient cause of all phenomena merely because volition is an efficient cause of bodily motions; such a generalization requires independent external evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poincaré argues that consciousness of volition does not provide a priori knowledge of causal efficacy beyond our own bodily actions; extrapolating that volition is the universal efficient cause is unjustified and an overreach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not base theory choice on conceivability or subjective feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Appeals to what is 'inconceivable' or 'naturally conceivable' to the mind are unreliable as evidence for or against causal theories, because conceivability is shaped by experience and habit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text shows that what seems conceivable varies historically and individually (Greeks, Cartesians, moderns); therefore, subjective conceivability cannot be elevated to an objective test for causal claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalize only from appropriately similar instances
rubrics_metrics.description: Inductive generalizations must be based on instances that resemble the known case; one should not extrapolate universal claims from a single dissimilar instance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: knowing that our world is inhabited does not justify concluding that all heavenly bodies are inhabited. Similarly, observing volition as a cause for bodily motion does not warrant concluding volition causes all phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require empirical/experiential support for asserted causal connections (no a priori claims of efficient causes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that certain kinds of causes (especially 'efficient causes' known a priori) exist must be supported by experience; consciousness of an internal state does not give a priori causal knowledge of external sequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poincaré challenges claims that consciousness of willing is an a priori justification for asserting efficient causation; paralysis and learned associations show such knowledge is empirical and fallible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical and evidential accuracy when using historical cases to support philosophical claims
rubrics_metrics.description: When invoking historical philosophers or cases to argue about conceivability or the history of ideas, ensure accurate scholarship and reliable sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supplementary note critiques an opponent's historical assertions (about Thales, Anaximenes) as erroneous; Poincaré stresses checking historians of philosophy rather than relying on secondary fancy (Cicero).
